paper_title: GlanceNav: Efficient Vision-and-Language Navigation with Streaming Memory and Counterfactual Rewind

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong policies for vision-and-language navigation (VLN). However, most of them encode a sample of past frames again at every decision and are trained on isolated decisions, so computation is redundant and the usable history is short. They also learn from their own mistakes through outcome rewards that give one scalar to a whole episode. We ask whether a navigator can encode each frame only once, at a constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its mistakes. We present GlanceNav, a streaming navigator built on a hybrid MLLM. Its Gated DeltaNet layers carry a recurrent state through the whole episode, while its attention layers keep a short window of recent observations and a small bank of keyframes, selected by how much each frame changes the recurrent state. This constant-size memory keeps the cost per step fixed and allows training on whole episodes with the same memory as at inference. Because the entire memory can also be copied in constant time, we further propose Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe), a reinforcement learning stage that rewinds a drifting rollout to its closest approach to the goal, lets an expert correct a few actions, and credits decisions by the resulting change in outcome. Trained only on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits, with 1,000 instructions for reinforcement learning, a 4B GlanceNav reaches success rates of 71.9% and 73.6% on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen. On R2R-CE, it outperforms the strongest previous single-RGB method trained without external data by 9.1 points, while running at 104 ms per step.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) [3, 18, 20] asks an agent to follow naturallanguage instruction through an unseen building, using only its egocentric observations. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now power most strong VLN-CE agents [5, 40, 4850]. Many of them treat navigation as video question answering (Fig. 1a): at every step, they sample fixed number of past frames, typically eight, and encode them again together with the current view. This design has two problems. The first is the memory: each frame is processed once for every later decision that samples it, the policy cannot see what falls outside the sample, and every decision is trained as separate sample. Streaming navigators avoid re-encoding by caching the key-value (KV) states of past observations [40, 56]. full cache, however, grows linearly with the episode, so these methods bound it with sliding windows and pruned or compressed memories. Bounding the cache fixes the cost but not the memory: eviction is final, and whatever leaves the cache is invisible to every later decision. The second problem is how the agent learns from its own mistakes. Beyond DAgger [27], recent navigators are fine-tuned with outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) such as GRPO [30, 55], which gives one scalar to all of the roughly one hundred decisions of rollout and learns mostly from instructions on which some rollouts succeed and others fail, which become rarer as the policy improves. We therefore ask: can navigator encode each frame only once, at constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its own mistakes? Hybrid MLLMs [11, 26, 45] remove the need to choose between cost and memory. Most of their layers are Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, which fold every token into fixed-size recurrent state, and only few are softmax attention. The whole episode is therefore always summarized in the state. The summary is lossy, so the few attention layers still need exact tokens, but only as complement. The memory question thus changes from which part of the history to keep to which few frames should also be kept exactly. GlanceNav (Fig. 1b) answers this question with the state itself. Its attention layers see window of the most recent observations and small bank of older keyframes, selected by state-change score: the relative change that frame causes in the recurrent state of the GDN layer below. frame that the state already predicts changes it little, whereas frame with new content, such as new room, changes it more and is kept. The score has no parameters. Two properties follow. The memory has constant size: each frame is encoded once, and step costs the same throughout an episode. It is also causal: keyframes are selected from the past only, so the memory of every step can be built inside one forward pass over an episode, and GlanceNav is trained on whole episodes with its test-time memory instead of on isolated decisions. The constant size also addresses the second problem: snapshot of the agents entire memory takes 136 MiB and 1.4 ms to copy, at any step, so rollout can be rewound to any earlier decision. Our Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe) detects when rollout starts to move away from the goal, restores the simulator and the agents memory at the rollouts closest approach to the goal, lets shortest-path expert redo few actions, and lets the policy finish. The difference in outcome between this branch and the original rollout then credits the policys continuation, and the experts actions only when the branch did better. drifting rollout thus yields contrast between two outcomes from the same state, instead of one scalar for the whole episode. We train GlanceNav in three stages, using only the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits: episode-level supervised fine-tuning (SFT), DAgger, and CoRe on 1,000 instructions. With 4B backbone, GlanceNav reaches 71.9% success rate (SR) on R2R-CE val-unseen and 73.6% on RxR-CE (Fig. 1c, Tab. 1). On R2R-CE, this is 9.1 points above the best previous single-RGB method trained without external data, and among all single-RGB methods that we compare with, only an 8B model trained with additional data scores higher. GlanceNav runs at 104 ms per step, less than half the step time of step-wise navigator with backbone of the same size (Tab. 2). Our contributions are: We propose constant-size streaming memory for hybrid MLLM navigators, which keeps keyframes selected by parameter-free state-change score, and an episode-level training scheme that matches deployment and encodes 8.6 fewer frames than step-wise training. We propose Counterfactual Rewind, an RL method that branches from rollouts closest approach to the goal using an (1) memory snapshot, and credits the experts corrections and the policys continuation by their counterfactual outcome. One pass over 1,000 instructions adds 8.2 SR to the DAgger-trained policy, against 3.1 for GRPO on the same instructions (Sec. 4.4). With 4B backbone and no external training data, GlanceNav reaches 71.9% and 73.6% SR on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen at constant 104 ms per step. sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Vision-language models for navigation. Early VLN-CE agents rely on panoramas, depth and waypoint predictors [13, 18, 19, 37]. Video MLLMs made navigation from single RGB camera competitive [5, 49, 50]. Later work scales the training data [51, 52], or adds self-correction data [47], dual-system planners [39, 43], geometry encoders [25, 48, 53], auxiliary objectives [7, 34, 57], agentic decomposition [42] or stereo input [35]. Most of these methods build each decision from resampled set of frames, and their best results use external data such as ScaleVLN [36], VQA or web video. GlanceNav keeps one persistent stream and uses no external data. Streaming and selective memory. StreamVLN [40] keeps sliding window of dialogue turns and pruned memory of older ones. JanusVLN [48] keeps the KV caches of the initial and the most recent frames from semantic and geometry encoder [31]. Efficient-VLN [56] reuses the KV cache as well and packs several decisions of trajectory into one training sequence. In LLMs and video models, KV-eviction methods keep tokens by recency, attention mass or query relevance [23, 41, 54]. Linear-attention and state-space layers replace the cache with fixed-size state [8, 10, 29, 44, 45], and hybrid models interleave them with few attention layers [17, 26]. Two recent works read the delta rule to decide which exact tokens to keep: HOLA [6] keeps tokens with large committed write, and the concurrent DeltaS [21] evicts video chunks by their state drift without training. Our state-change score belongs to this family. Unlike these works, which target language and video understanding, we train navigation policy end to end with the resulting memory and evaluate it in closed-loop control. Learning from policy errors. DAgger [27] labels the states visited by the learner and is widely used by MLLM navigators [40, 48, 56]. ActiveVLN [55] trains an MLLM navigator with multi-turn GRPO [30], which we adopt as our RL baseline. Recent methods make its sparse outcome reward more informative: SACA [22] resamples from divergence point found by an auditor, SeekVLN [38] contrasts counterfactual branches at evidence-seeking steps, and BudVLN [12] rectifies failures from the farthest progress along the reference path. Branching from intermediate states is also used in LLM reasoning [15], exploration [9] and test-time backtracking for VLN [16]. CoRe branches at the closest approach to the goal, restores the full streaming memory there in (1), and imitates the expert only when its branch outperforms the original rollout, Q-filter [24] estimated by rollout instead of learned critic.

The agent observes 480640 RGB images, moves forward 0.25 or turns 15 per action, and succeeds if it stops within 3 of the goal. Following standard practice, we report navigation error (NE), oracle success (OS), success rate (SR) and success weighted by path length (SPL) [2], and on RxR-CE also normalized dynamic time warping (nDTW) [14]. sections.title: 4.3 Ablation Study
sections.content: Streaming memory. Table 5 trains Stage-1 model for each memory. Adding bank of four keyframes to the four-step window raises SR from 48.7 to 52.4. The gain depends on what the bank holds. Averaging the token scores of frame gives 49.3, close to the window alone, and under an earlier training schedule, bank of randomly chosen tokens did not help at all, whereas scored bank of the same size raised SR from 46.3 to 49.3 (Tab. 6). Among the better scores, the differences are small. Keeping tokens by their committed write, as in HOLA [6], or by learned ranker gives 51.7, and our frame-level score is not significantly better (𝑝=0.59, exact McNemar test). We use 𝛿𝑠 because it keeps whole frames, has no parameters, and has the clear reading of Eq. (4). Scoring rule. Table 5 compares ten parameter-free scores read from the GDN layer below each attention layer, and two learned rankers trained to predict tokens future attention mass. The frame-level state-change score of Eq. (2) gives the highest SR. However, the SR of the ten GDN-derived scores has standard deviation of only 1.1 points (49.0 to 52.4). Neither learned ranker improves on the parameter-free scores. Averaging the committed write over frame is the worst frame-level rule, so the result is not explained by frame granularity alone. Random bank. Under an earlier schedule (the epoch-1 checkpoint of two-epoch run), we compared random and scored banks directly (Tab. 6). bank of random old tokens does not help (0.2 against the window alone, 𝑝=0.90), whereas bank of the same size filled by the committed write raises SR from 46.3 to 49.3 (𝑝=0.023) and beats the random bank by 3.2 points (𝑝=0.018). Moving budget from the window to the bank helps further, and ninth recent step, which costs about as much as one-frame bank, lowers SR. The policy also relies on its bank: serving the committed-write model of Tab. 5 without its bank costs 1.7 points (𝑝=0.12). 9 GlanceNav: Efficient Vision-and-Language Navigation with Streaming Memory and Counterfactual Rewind Table 8. Table 7 trains model for each budget. With eight visible frames, window of four steps and four keyframes outperforms window of eight steps by 3.4 SR on R2R-CE and 1.3 on RxR-CE, and window alone needs twelve frames to come close (51.2 and 56.7). On R2R-CE, larger bank or window does not help further (51.3 and 51.0). On RxR-CE, the banks with 𝑊=4 lie within 1.7 points of each other, and two keyframes score highest. We keep 𝑊=4 and 𝐹=4, the best budget on R2R-CE. Figure 4 plots the eight models of Tab. 7 against the number of frames visible to an attention layer. Starting from the four-step window, the next frames help more as keyframes than as recent steps on both benchmarks: with six or eight visible frames, every model with bank outperforms the window-only models, and window alone needs twelve frames to be on par. The split matters as well. window of two steps with four keyframes is 3.2 points below 𝑊=4 on R2R-CE (0.4 on RxR-CE), and window of eight steps does not improve on 𝑊=4 either. DAgger labels and data. We follow the recovery protocol of JanusVLN [48]: the Stage-1 policy drives greedily on the training instructions, and shortest-path expert takes over after clear failures and returns control to the policy at the next waypoint. Because the memory of GlanceNav contains its own responses, takeover restores the memory snapshot taken after the observation and appends the experts response instead of the learners. Inputs, recurrent state and bank are therefore those of the executed trajectory. We keep episodes that end at the goal and contain detour, which gives 14,195 episodes with 1.61M steps. In 31% of the collected steps, the executed action is mistake of the learner made before takeover, so supervising the executed actions imitates these mistakes. We therefore keep the input stream bit-exact, so that recurrent state and bank match the rollout, and replace only the targets by the experts action at every visited state (oracle relabeling). During collection, the expert also overrides the learners STOP proposals until the agent is very close to the goal, so near the goal both labels say keep moving. We truncate each episode at the learners first STOP proposal near the goal and label that step STOP (STOP correction). We train for one epoch from the Stage-1 weights on the DAgger episodes together with the expert demonstrations of the 16,620 training instructions for which no DAgger episode was kept, so that every instruction appears once (30,815 episodes in total). Table 8 shows that both the labels and the demonstrations matter. Supervising executed actions does not improve SR, although the agent reaches the goal area far more often (OS 58.070.3), because it also learns the learners mistakes and the experts refusals to stop. Oracle relabeling adds 6.8 points with the same inputs. DAgger episodes alone lead to long paths (15.1 m). Adding demonstrations restores path efficiency and gives the best model.

sections.content: Setup. Every RL run starts from the Stage-2 model and makes one pass over 1,000 instructions. GRPO and CoRe see the same instructions in the same order, with the same seed: the first 500 of the R2R-CE list and of the RxR-CE list released with ActiveVLN [55], without any selection. This is 3% of our training instructions and an eighth of those that ActiveVLN uses. GRPO follows the recipe of ActiveVLN, and CoRe adds its branches to it. We report one training run per setting. Training stages. Table 9 shows that every stage helps. DAgger raises SR from 52.4 to 63.7. This requires labeling every visited state with the experts action; supervising the executed actions instead leaves SR unchanged (Tab. 8). CoRe then adds 8.2 points in 12.5 on two GPUs. RxR-CE improves with every stage as well, from 56.6 to 67.2 and 73.6 SR. CoRe vs. GRPO. sections.title: 4.5 Real-World Experiments
sections.content: We deploy GlanceNav on Unitree G1 humanoid robot equipped with chest-mounted ZED Mini camera, using only the left RGB stream. workstation with an RTX 5090 runs the navigation policy and receives observations over Wi-Fi. All real-world experiments are conducted without fine-tuning on real-world data. The instructions fall into two categories: (i) T1 (Moderate-length Navigation), which requires the robot to distinguish visually similar objects and use their spatial or sequential relationships to identify the correct stopping location; and (ii) T2 (Long-range Navigation), which requires landmark recognition and navigation decisions at multiple points along the route. Figure 7 shows one successful episode of each category, in which the robot recognizes the landmarks and stops at the described location. More real-world results are in App. A.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented GlanceNav, VLN agent that encodes each frame once and keeps constant-size streaming memory: the recurrent state of hybrid MLLM, short window of recent observations, and bank of keyframes that changed the state the most. Because the memory is causal and bounded, GlanceNav is trained on whole episodes with its deployment memory, runs at constant cost per step, and can copy its full memory in (1). Counterfactual Rewind uses these copies to correct drifting rollouts at their closest approach to the goal and to give counterfactual credit to corrections and continuations. Using only the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits and 1,000 RL instructions, 4B GlanceNav reaches 71.9 SR on R2R-CE val-unseen and 73.6 on RxR-CE at 104 ms per step.
